evidence_items.explanation: Supports the narrower observation that MathGLM remained unreliable as arithmetic inputs grew. The experiment added 50,000 training records within the 12-digit range, so its declining performance does not itself establish a universal inability to extrapolate beyond training lengths.

evidence_items.locator: Section 3, addition experiments and discussion of Table 1
evidence_items.explanation: Material counterevidence to an absolute absence of extrapolation: models trained on five-digit addition reached 99.9% accuracy at ten digits and 98.3% at fifteen. Accuracy fell to 21.3% at twenty digits, so this does not establish the sustained reliability emphasized by Marcus.

evidence_items.publisher: Shaoxiong Duan and Yining Shi, arXiv
evidence_items.locator: Section 6, Main Results; methods in Section 5 and training-length comparison in Figure 1
evidence_items.explanation: The original report describes substantial extrapolation, including addition trained through six digits, using attention patterns extracted, extended, and incorporated into retraining. This challenges the broader claim about transformer learning, but whether these specialized calibrated models qualify as pure LLMs is unresolved.

unresolved_gaps: MathGLM's measured failures do not establish the categorical claim across pure LLMs.
The strongest contemporaneous extrapolation result uses specialized attention calibration; the source claim does not settle whether that falls inside its model scope.
The records examined do not establish a qualifying pure LLM with sustained exact arithmetic extrapolation under the full contextual reading.
Finite benchmark success or failure alone does not establish whether a complete arithmetic algorithm was learned.
